proposals.relationship: Harris uses Said’s account of European categories to explain how fur traders organized their opposition between civilization and savagery.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1997–98 article 59/n 39 calls Orientalism the original and most influential discussion of the categories described in the preceding paragraph. Harris applies this resource to traders’ conceptual coordination while distinguishing their circumstances from European legal sovereignty 58. This specific use coexists with his later criticism of giving cultural discourse excessive explanatory weight, already 1017; neither wholesale adherence nor a critique directed solely at Said is asserted. Original Orientalism and the complete 2004 article remain unread.

proposals.relationship: MacDonald and Wynn with Barnes identify Innis’s spatial economy as a particular resource for Harris’s framing of the collective Historical Atlas of Canada.
proposals.evidence_note: MacDonald’s complete 1990 review quotes Harris’s preface invoking Innis’s account of Canada’s long spatial development through staple trades and transport, and distinguishing its pattern from the United States. Wynn and Barnes 2023:3 independently describe the volume’s dedication to Innis for spatial economy and to Andrew H. Clark for settlement and the local region. The Atlas belongs to its many contributors and cartographers, including Geoffrey J. Matthews; Clark retains equal credit for a distinct pole. This is an explicitly mediated resource, not a new reading of the original Atlas preface or Innis, and not all contributors’ sole intellectual genealogy.

proposals.relationship: Wynn and Barnes describe Harris’s engagement with Habermas, alongside Foucault and others, as sharpening his understanding while he brought social theory into historical geography.
proposals.evidence_note: Wynn and Barnes 2023:3 place this engagement within post-Atlas discussions with UBC colleagues and graduate students, and cite Harris’s 1991 call for conversation between historical geography and social theory. Their explicit account of theoretical clarification supports a bounded, named scholarly resource. Foucault retains separate equal credit and his already 1018 specific use; no singular origin, direct teaching, personal contact or detailed adoption of every Habermasian concept is inferred. Harris’s complete 1991 and 2008 articles and Habermas’s originals were not available as actual bodies through the checked routes and remain unread.
